screens.title: Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) Fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: In this module we will unpack Public Key Infrastructure, or PKI, the operational framework that makes public-key cryptography usable across an organization. PKI is more than keys and certificates: it combines trusted authorities, registration processes, repositories, and revocation mechanisms so that devices, users, and services can authenticate and encrypt reliably. You will learn how a root Certificate Authority establishes trust, why intermediates reduce operational risk, what a Registration Authority does, and how certificates are published and checked with CRLs and OCSP. We'll also examine the structure of an X.509 certificate — fields like Subject, Issuer, SAN, Key Usage, and Extended Key Usage — and why those fields matter when a browser or client decides to trust a connection. By the end, you'll be able to describe PKI components, choose an appropriate trust model for enterprise deployment, and explain how revocation choices affect security and availability. Consider how a single mismanaged certificate could cause a major outage; we will avoid that by learning sound policies and checks.

screens.title: PKI architecture and components
screens.narratorSegment: PKI is a system of people, processes, and technology. At its center is the Certificate Authority, the entity that signs and issues X.509 certificates, creating trust anchors with its signature. Root CAs sit at the top and are typically offline to reduce attack surface. Intermediate CAs are signed by the root and handle day-to-day issuance, which lets the organization revoke or replace intermediates without touching the root. A Registration Authority can act as a verification broker, checking subscriber identity, collecting certificate requests, and forwarding validated requests to the CA — this keeps the CA tightly controlled. A repository publishes certificates and revocation data, often via LDAP or HTTP, so relying parties can retrieve what they need. Finally, OCSP responders provide real-time revocation answers. Misunderstanding these components leads to risky designs; for example, placing issuance logic on the root CA exposes the trust anchor to operational compromise. A secure architecture keeps the root minimally accessible, uses intermediates for operational flexibility, and employs an RA to centralize identity checks. PKI architecture and components means design pki so the root is protected, intermediates handle operations, and supporting services publish status and revocation cleanly.. In practical terms, how authorities, repositories, and responders form a trustworthy system. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › PKI architecture
Core Concept
PKI components and role separation

A secure PKI splits duties to limit risk. The root CA is the ultimate trust anchor; intermediates handle issuance; RAs validate identities; repositories and responders share or attest status.

  • Root CA: offline trust anchor that signs intermediates.
  • Intermediate CA: operational signer for end-entity certificates.
  • RA: verifies requester identity and forwards validated CSRs.
  • Repository/Responder: publish certificates/CRLs and answer OCSP queries.
Key Takeaway

Separate duties so the root stays inert and operations run from intermediates and RAs. That reduces scope and supports recovery.

Architecture diagram (card-first)
Root CA (offline)
Signs intermediate CA certificates. Kept offline and securely backed up.
Intermediate CA (online)
Performs issuance and can be revoked or replaced without touching the root.
Registration Authority
Validates identity, collects CSRs, and queues issuance tasks for the CA.
Repository
Publishes certificates and CRLs for retrieval by clients or administrators.
OCSP Responder
Answers real-time revocation queries; supports stapling to improve client performance.
Misconception: OCSP replaces CRLs entirely. Contrast: OCSP is real-time but depends on responder availability and design choices.

screens.title: Certificate Authority roles — Root vs Intermediate
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the distinction between root and intermediate CAs is fundamental. A root CA is the ultimate trust anchor: its public key is distributed to clients as a trusted root, and any certificate chain traced back to it can be trusted. Because of this centrality, organizations typically keep root CA private keys offline and highly protected, using them only to sign intermediate CA certificates. Intermediate CAs hold certificates signed by the root and perform day-to-day issuance. This tiered approach brings operational benefits: if an intermediate is compromised, the organization can revoke that intermediate and reissue without needing to replace the root. It also allows different intermediates to enforce policy boundaries — for example, one intermediate for server certificates, another for code signing. A common misconception is that fewer CAs equals simpler security; in reality, a single online root increases risk. Tiered design balances security with operational flexibility and supports key rotation and compartmentalization. Certificate Authority roles — Root vs Intermediate means use an offline root and online intermediates to minimize compromise impact and enable operational rotation.. In practical terms, why tiered signing reduces risk and supports recovery. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Root vs Intermediate
Definition
Root and intermediate CA roles

The root CA is the trust anchor. Intermediates, signed by the root, handle issuance. This separation supports compartmentalization and safe recovery.

Root CA: Trusted by clients, kept offline, used sparingly to sign intermediate certificates.
Intermediate CA: Signs end-entity certificates, can be revoked or replaced to limit blast radius.
Operational tip: Use purpose-separated intermediates for server authentication, client auth, and code signing.
Common Mistake

Putting issuance logic on the root CA increases risk because the root key is then exposed to operational systems. Keep the root inert.

Hierarchy example
Root CA (offline)
Signs Intermediate CA certificates during planned ceremonies.
Intermediate A: Server TLS
Handles TLS certificates, enforces stricter issuance policy and shorter lifetimes.
Intermediate B: Code Signing
Separate policy to restrict key usage and reduce cross-impact from compromise.

screens.title: Registration Authority (RA)
screens.narratorSegment: The Registration Authority is an intermediary that verifies the identity of certificate requesters before the CA issues a certificate. An RA collects the Certificate Signing Request and the proof documents or authentication data needed to confirm identity, then forwards validated requests to the CA. Using an RA is a practical measure to protect the CA: the CA can remain offline or tightly restricted, while the RA performs the higher-volume identity checks. For example, an RA may validate employee directories, check ownership of a domain, or verify corporate registrations depending on the certificate type. A misconception is that the RA is optional in all deployments; while small, single-application PKIs may omit a dedicated RA, enterprise-grade PKI commonly uses RAs to centralize and auditable identity verification. An effective RA implementation includes logging, role separation, and strong process controls so that identity checks themselves cannot be bypassed or forged. Registration Authority (RA) means let the ra handle identity verification so the ca can be constrained and protected from direct operational exposure.. In practical terms, verifying identity so the ca can remain secure. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Registration Authority
Definition
What an RA does

An RA verifies identities and forwards validated certificate signing requests to the CA, enabling the CA to remain controlled and secure.

  • Verify identity: documents, directory records, or domain ownership checks.
  • Collect CSRs: ensure keys and request data are correctly formed before submission to CA.
  • Audit trail: logging verification steps supports later investigation and compliance.
Misconception

The RA is not merely optional in enterprise PKI; it is often required to centralize trusted identity checks and enforce policy.

Example: employee certificate issuance
An employee requests a client authentication certificate. The RA verifies HR records and a corporate email challenge, records evidence, and forwards the CSR to an intermediate CA for issuance.
Step 1
Collect CSR
User generates key pair and CSR, submits to RA.
Step 2
Verify identity
RA checks HR and email ownership and logs evidence.

screens.title: Certificate Revocation — CRL
screens.narratorSegment: A Certificate Revocation List, or CRL, is a signed, timestamped list containing serial numbers of certificates that a CA has invalidated before their scheduled expiration. CAs publish CRLs at regular intervals so relying parties can download and compare certificates they encounter to the list of revoked serial numbers. Because CRLs are periodically published, there is an inherent delay between revocation and when clients download the updated list; this window creates exposure if a compromised certificate continues to be accepted until the next CRL download. CRLs are useful where clients can cache lists and where offline validation is acceptable. They are simple to implement and do not require an online responder, but they can become large in high-volume environments and increase bandwidth and processing requirements. Operational practice includes setting reasonable publication frequency, using delta CRLs where supported to reduce size, and combining CRLs with other mechanisms for timely revocation when necessary. Certificate Revocation — CRL means crls are periodic lists of revoked certificates; simple and offline-friendly but can be stale and heavy at scale.. In practical terms, how certificate revocation lists are published and consumed. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: CRLs are periodic lists of revoked certificates; simple and offline-friendly but can be stale and heavy at scale.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Certificate Revocation List
Process Flow
CRL publication and consumption

A CA compiles revoked certificate serial numbers into a signed CRL and publishes it to a repository. Clients download the CRL on a schedule and check certificate serials against it.

  1. CA revokes a certificate and appends its serial number to the CRL.
  2. CA publishes the signed CRL to an accessible repository (HTTP/LDAP).
  3. Clients periodically download or check cached CRLs when validating certificates.
Pro Tip

Use delta CRLs where possible to reduce download size, and set publication intervals that balance bandwidth and timeliness.

Example scenario
A web server's private key is suspected of compromise. The CA revokes the certificate and publishes a new CRL. Clients that download the updated CRL will reject the compromised certificate once their cache refreshes.
Key downside
Staleness window: until clients fetch the new CRL, the revoked certificate may still be accepted.
When to use
Environments where clients can cache lists and online responders are unavailable or undesirable.

screens.title: OCSP and OCSP stapling
screens.narratorSegment: OCSP, the Online Certificate Status Protocol, provides a way for clients to query a responder in real time about the revocation status of a specific certificate. Instead of downloading an entire list, a client asks the OCSP responder whether a certificate is good, revoked, or unknown. This reduces bandwidth and provides near real-time answers. OCSP stapling further improves performance and privacy: the server fetches a signed OCSP response from the responder and presents it during the TLS handshake. This means the client receives revocation status without contacting the OCSP responder directly, lowering latency and avoiding client-side privacy leaks. However, OCSP introduces a dependency on responder availability; if the responder is unreachable, clients and servers must have policy decisions about how to proceed. A misconception is that OCSP always eliminates staleness; while it is more timely than CRLs, its reliability depends on responder design and caching behavior. Practitioners often combine OCSP, stapling, and robust responder deployment for both timeliness and resilience. OCSP and OCSP stapling means ocsp gives timely revocation status; stapling reduces client latency and privacy exposure but requires careful responder availability planning.. In practical terms, real-time revocation checks and performance considerations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: OCSP gives timely revocation status; stapling reduces client latency and privacy exposure but requires careful responder availability planning.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › OCSP & Stapling
Process Flow
OCSP real-time checks

Clients query an OCSP responder with a certificate serial number; the responder returns a signed status of good, revoked, or unknown. Stapling reduces client burden by letting servers present a recent signed OCSP response during handshake.

Client query: client -> OCSP responder -> signed status returned.
Stapling: server fetches signed response and includes it in TLS handshake.
Trade-offs: timeliness vs responder availability and complexity.
Concrete example
A web server configures OCSP stapling so its clients receive revocation status with no extra round trip. If the responder fails, the server may present a cached OCSP response, but operators must decide fail-open vs fail-closed policy based on risk tolerance.
Pro Tip
Deploy redundant responders and monitor stapling freshness to avoid serving stale status or causing handshake failures.
Misconception
OCSP always fixes revocation staleness. In practice, it depends on responder reachability and cache lifetimes.

screens.title: X.509 certificate anatomy
screens.narratorSegment: An X.509 certificate binds a public key to an identity and defines how that key may be used. Key fields include Subject — the entity the certificate represents — and Issuer — the CA that signed the certificate. The public key itself is included, plus a unique serial number the CA uses to track the certificate. Validity dates define the window during which the certificate is considered valid. The Signature Algorithm indicates how the CA signed the certificate. Extensions add policy and constraints: Subject Alternative Name allows multiple hostnames or addresses to be covered; Key Usage defines allowed cryptographic operations like digital signature or key encipherment; Extended Key Usage narrows the certificate to particular applications such as Server Authentication or Code Signing. Reading these fields helps you determine whether a certificate suits a purpose and whether a client should trust it. A common oversight is relying on expiry alone; extensions and SANs often determine whether a certificate will be accepted by clients. X.509 certificate anatomy means subject, issuer, public key, serial, validity, signature, and extensions together determine a certificate’s identity and permitted uses.. In practical terms, fields that bind keys to identities and control use. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › X.509 Anatomy
Definition
Key certificate fields

Read these fields to confirm identity, purpose, and validity of a certificate before trusting it in production.

Subject: the entity (person, server, or organization) the cert represents.
Issuer: the CA that signed the certificate.
Public Key / Serial: the public key and a unique serial for tracking.
Validity: notBefore and notAfter define the accepted window.
Signature Algorithm: shows how the CA signed the certificate.
Important extensions
Subject Alternative Name (SAN)
Allows multiple hostnames or addresses in a single certificate; required for modern TLS.
Key Usage
Specifies cryptographic purposes, e.g., digitalSignature, keyEncipherment.
Extended Key Usage (EKU)
Limits the certificate to applications like Server Authentication or Code Signing.
Key Takeaway

Extensions determine acceptance. Check SAN and EKU carefully when diagnosing connection failures or policy mismatches.

screens.title: SAN, Key Usage, and EKU explained
screens.narratorSegment: Three certificate extensions are especially relevant for operational compatibility: Subject Alternative Name, Key Usage, and Extended Key Usage. SAN lists all DNS names and IPs a certificate covers; if a client checks the server hostname against the certificate and the SAN does not include that name, the client will report a name mismatch. Key Usage controls cryptographic actions, for example whether a key can be used to encrypt keys or to perform a digital signature. EKU provides more explicit application-level constraints: a certificate may have EKU set to Server Authentication so it can be used for TLS, or Code Signing so it can sign binaries. Together these extensions prevent certificates from being misapplied. For instance, a code-signing certificate without Server Authentication EKU should not be trusted by a web server. A common error is relying solely on Subject CN for hostname matching; modern clients prioritize SAN and may ignore CN for multi-name certificates. When issuing certificates, ensure SAN entries and EKU align with the intended use to avoid client errors and security gaps. SAN, Key Usage, and EKU explained means san controls hostnames, key usage controls cryptographic operations, and eku limits the certificate to specific application contexts.. In practical terms, how these extensions affect hostname matching and permitted operations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › SAN, Key Usage, EKU
Comparison
SAN vs Key Usage vs EKU

Each extension answers a different question: "Which names are valid?", "What cryptographic operations are allowed?", and "Which applications may use this cert?".

Subject Alternative Name (SAN)
Controls hostnames/IPs. Required for multi-domain TLS.
Key Usage
Indicates allowed crypto operations like digitalSignature, keyEncipherment.
Extended Key Usage (EKU)
Limits application contexts such as Server Authentication or Code Signing.
Concrete example
If you issue one certificate for app.internal.example.com and legacy-app.internal.example.com, include both names in SAN. Also set EKU to Server Authentication and Key Usage to keyEncipherment and digitalSignature so TLS clients accept it for HTTPS.
Misconception
Relying on the certificate Subject CN alone is insufficient on modern clients; always populate SAN for multi-name certificates.
Key Takeaway
Align SAN, Key Usage, and EKU to the intended service to prevent acceptance failures and limit misuse.

screens.title: PKI trust models
screens.narratorSegment: Choose a trust model based on scale, federation needs, and administrative control. The hierarchical model uses a single root that signs intermediates; trust flows downward and is easy to reason about — this is dominant in enterprise PKI because it centralizes authority and simplifies revocation decisions. The mesh model, or cross-certification, has CAs directly trusting each other and is useful in federated environments where peers establish bilateral trust relationships. It trades simplicity for flexibility and requires careful planning to avoid trust cycles or unexpected trust paths. The bridge model introduces a central bridge CA that connects separate hierarchies without requiring direct cross-certificates between every pair; this supports federation without collapsing local control. Each model affects certificate validation, revocation complexity, and operational procedures. For instance, cross-certification complicates revocation checks because trust paths may span multiple administrative domains. When designing an enterprise PKI, favor the hierarchical model for internal services and consider bridge patterns only when inter-organization trust is required. PKI trust models means hierarchical gives clear control and simpler revocation; mesh and bridge support federation but add complexity and planning overhead.. In practical terms, hierarchical, mesh, and bridge — trade-offs and enterprise implications. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Trust Models
Hierarchical
Single root, intermediates below. Clear trust path and centralized policy. Preferred for internal enterprise PKI.
Mesh (Cross-certification)
CAs trust each other directly. Useful for peer federation but increases complexity in path discovery and revocation.
Bridge
A bridge CA mediates trust between hierarchies. Maintains local autonomy while enabling cross-domain trust.
Operational note
Federated models require careful certificate path analysis and coordinated revocation procedures. Prefer hierarchical where you control most participants.

screens.title: Certificate lifecycle
screens.narratorSegment: The certificate lifecycle has distinct stages that each require policy and operational controls. It begins with key generation and a Certificate Signing Request. The RA or CA validates identity and issues the certificate. The certificate is then distributed to the subscriber and published to a repository. During usage, the certificate participates in protocols like TLS where clients validate its chain and extensions. Before expiry, certificates should be renewed — often with a new key pair — to maintain continuity and reduce risk from long-lived keys. If compromise or role change occurs, the certificate must be revoked and that revocation published via CRL or OCSP. Finally, expiry ends the certificate’s validity. Mismanaging any stage causes outages or security incidents: failing to renew leads to service failure, while failing to revoke a compromised certificate leaves systems vulnerable. Robust lifecycle management includes monitoring impending expirations, automated renewal where appropriate, clear revocation procedures, and periodic audits. Certificate lifecycle means treat each lifecycle stage as an operational checkpoint: generate securely, verify identity, publish status, renew proactively, and revoke when needed.. In practical terms, from csr generation through expiration — stages and controls. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Treat each lifecycle stage as an operational checkpoint: generate securely, verify identity, publish status, renew proactively, and revoke when needed.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Certificate Lifecycle
Timeline
Stages of a certificate
  1. Generation/Issuance: generate key pair, create CSR, verify identity, issue.
  2. Distribution: deliver cert to holder and publish to repository.
  3. Usage: certificate used in protocols like TLS or code signing.
  4. Renewal: replace expiring certs, usually with new keys.
  5. Revocation: react immediately to compromise or invalidation.
  6. Expiration: certificate becomes invalid after its validity period.
Key Takeaway

Operationalize monitoring and automation for renewals and revocations to avoid outages and reduce compromise windows.

Example — renewal vs revocation
Plan renewals weeks before expiry with automated workflows. If a private key is stolen, revoke immediately and publish status via OCSP or CRL to prevent misuse.
Operational checklist
Monitor expirations, test revocation checks, document RA procedures, and restrict root CA access.
Common error
Neglecting revocation publication frequency leads to stale acceptance of compromised certificates.

screens.title: Revocation in practice — CRL vs OCSP decision guide
screens.narratorSegment: Deciding between CRL and OCSP requires weighing timeliness, scalability, and availability. CRLs are simple: the CA periodically publishes a list clients download. They work well where clients can reliably fetch and cache lists and where occasionally stale status is acceptable. OCSP offers near real-time answers and is preferred when quick revocation is critical — for example, after private key compromise on a high-value server. OCSP stapling reduces client load by letting servers present a recent response during handshake, improving latency and privacy. Hybrid approaches are common: CRLs as a baseline with OCSP for critical services. Also consider delta CRLs to decrease list size. Operational constraints matter: if you cannot guarantee responder uptime or network reachability from clients, leaning on CRLs may be more dependable. Ultimately, document policies that state acceptable staleness windows, required responder redundancy, and monitoring for both methods so revocations take effect in a predictable timeframe. Revocation in practice — CRL vs OCSP decision guide means match revocation method to risk: use ocsp for timely invalidation of critical certs and crls or delta crls for offline or high-scale scenarios.. In practical terms, when to prefer crl, ocsp, or a hybrid approach. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Match revocation method to risk: use OCSP for timely invalidation of critical certs and CRLs or delta CRLs for offline or high-scale scenarios.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Revocation Guide
Decision factors
  • Timeliness: OCSP is faster; CRLs can be stale.
  • Scale: CRLs can become large; OCSP scales better for individual checks but needs responder capacity.
  • Availability: OCSP depends on responder uptime; CRLs depend on client ability to fetch lists.
  • Privacy: OCSP reveals which certificates a client checks unless stapled by server.
Recommendation
Use OCSP for high-value, time-sensitive certificates and CRLs or delta CRLs where client reachability or responder availability is limited. Combine stapling to reduce client load and privacy leaks.
Example scenarios
If a TLS server private key is stolen, OCSP with stapling helps ensure clients reject the cert quickly. For isolated IoT devices with intermittent connectivity, delta CRLs may be more practical.
Checklist
Define staleness SLA, deploy redundant responders, log revocation events, and test client behavior under responder failure.
Misconception
Selecting OCSP alone guarantees safety. Without redundancy and monitoring, responder outages can cause validation failures or force fail-open behavior.

screens.title: Inspecting an X.509 certificate with openssl
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on walkthrough shows how to fetch and inspect a server certificate using the openssl command-line tools. First, use the s_client command to connect to the server and output the certificate chain; save the results to a PEM file. Then use openssl x509 with the text flag to render human-readable fields like Subject, Issuer, Validity, and extensions such as X509v3 Subject Alternative Name, Key Usage, and Extended Key Usage. Examining these outputs helps you confirm whether a certificate matches the expected hostnames and permitted functions. For example, the SAN extension lists hostnames covered by the certificate; Key Usage tells you if the key can perform key encipherment, and EKU indicates if the certificate is valid for Server Authentication. A typical mistake is to scan only the Subject CN and miss SAN entries. Practice on a well-known site and compare the chain to ensure intermediates are present. Always interpret openssl output in context of your validation policies. Inspecting an X.509 certificate with openssl means use openssl s_client and openssl x509 to retrieve and parse certificates, confirming fields and extensions required for trust.. In practical terms, retrieve a server certificate and examine subject, issuer, san, key usage, and eku. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Openssl Walkthrough
Hands-on Activity
Fetch and inspect a TLS certificate

Use the s_client command to retrieve the chain and save to a file, then read server certificate details with openssl x509 -text.

# Retrieve the certificate chain and save to a PEM file
openssl s_client -connect www.google.com:443 -servername www.google.com \
    -showcerts -print_certs -verify_hostname www.google.com -verify_return_error \
    < /dev/null 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -outform PEM > google_cert_chain.pem

# Inspect the first certificate in the chain
openssl x509 -in google_cert_chain.pem -noout -text

# Look for fields: Subject, Issuer, Validity, X509v3 Subject Alternative Name,
# X509v3 Key Usage, and X509v3 Extended Key Usage.
Note: interpret the output to confirm SAN entries and permitted EKUs. If a required name is missing in SAN, clients will report a name mismatch.
Example interpretation
After running the commands, check for X509v3 Subject Alternative Name to find covered hostnames. Confirm Key Usage includes digitalSignature if the certificate is used in TLS handshakes for signing, and EKU includes Server Authentication.
Check your understanding
If the SAN does not list legacy-app.internal.example.com, what will a client connecting to that hostname report? (Hint: a name mismatch).
Key Takeaway
Practice interpreting openssl output to link fields to policy decisions, such as whether a certificate is suitable for a given service.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Remember these core ideas as you design or evaluate PKI. First, the Certificate Authority is the trust anchor; design your hierarchy so the root is protected and intermediates handle operations. Second, an RA centralizes identity vetting so the CA can remain tightly controlled. Third, X.509 certificates include critical fields and extensions — SAN, Key Usage, and Extended Key Usage — that determine which names and operations a certificate supports. Fourth, revocation must be planned: CRLs are periodic and suitable where offline lists are acceptable, while OCSP provides timely status with performance and availability implications. Finally, manage the certificate lifecycle proactively: monitor expirations, automate renewals where possible, and publish revocations immediately. These points guide secure and resilient PKI operations and prevent common failures like name mismatches, stale revocation data, and overexposed root keys.

fullNarratorScript:
In this module we will unpack Public Key Infrastructure, or PKI, the operational framework that makes public-key cryptography usable across an organization. PKI is more than keys and certificates: it combines trusted authorities, registration processes, repositories, and revocation mechanisms so that devices, users, and services can authenticate and encrypt reliably. You will learn how a root Certificate Authority establishes trust, why intermediates reduce operational risk, what a Registration Authority does, and how certificates are published and checked with CRLs and OCSP. We'll also examine the structure of an X.509 certificate — fields like Subject, Issuer, SAN, Key Usage, and Extended Key Usage — and why those fields matter when a browser or client decides to trust a connection. Finally, we'll walk a certificate through its lifecycle: issuance, distribution, use, renewal, revocation, and expiration, and practice inspecting a real certificate with openssl. By the end, you'll be able to describe PKI components, choose an appropriate trust model for enterprise deployment, and explain how revocation choices affect security and availability. Consider how a single mismanaged certificate could cause a major outage; we will avoid that by learning sound policies and checks.

These objectives target the practical knowledge you need to operate or design PKI in an enterprise. First, you will identify core PKI components — root and intermediate CAs, RAs, repositories, CRLs, and OCSP — and describe how they interact to provide trust. Second, you will explain the X.509 certificate structure, recognizing fields and extensions such as Subject, Issuer, Subject Alternative Name, Key Usage, and Extended Key Usage, and why each field influences validation decisions. Third, you will differentiate trust models — hierarchical, mesh, and bridge — and understand the security and operational implications of choosing one in a real environment. Fourth, you will outline the certificate lifecycle from generation and issuance to renewal, revocation, and expiration, including the practical impact of revocation delays. Each objective combines conceptual understanding with operational significance so you can reason about risk, availability, and policy decisions. Throughout the chapter we’ll use concrete examples, like how SAN prevents hostname mismatches and why OCSP stapling improves performance and timeliness. These skills let you assess existing PKI deployments and propose improvements with confidence.

These applied objectives connect concepts to action. You will be able to inspect and interpret a live X.509 certificate using openssl, identifying Subject, Issuer, validity, SAN, Key Usage, and EKU fields. You will be able to explain why including a SAN entry prevents hostname mismatch errors and how EKU limits a certificate to server or code-signing use. You will also assess revocation strategies: determine when CRLs are sufficient and when OCSP, possibly with stapling, is necessary to meet timeliness and performance requirements. Finally, you will describe a secure CA hierarchy: why an offline root and online intermediates minimize the attack surface and how an RA supports identity verification without exposing the root. These outcomes prepare you to audit an internal PKI, advise on deployment architecture, and respond effectively to compromises by choosing the appropriate revocation and publication mechanisms.

PKI is a system of people, processes, and technology. At its center is the Certificate Authority, the entity that signs and issues X.509 certificates, creating trust anchors with its signature. Root CAs sit at the top and are typically offline to reduce attack surface. Intermediate CAs are signed by the root and handle day-to-day issuance, which lets the organization revoke or replace intermediates without touching the root. A Registration Authority can act as a verification broker, checking subscriber identity, collecting certificate requests, and forwarding validated requests to the CA — this keeps the CA tightly controlled. A repository publishes certificates and revocation data, often via LDAP or HTTP, so relying parties can retrieve what they need. Finally, OCSP responders provide real-time revocation answers. Misunderstanding these components leads to risky designs; for example, placing issuance logic on the root CA exposes the trust anchor to operational compromise. A secure architecture keeps the root minimally accessible, uses intermediates for operational flexibility, and employs an RA to centralize identity checks. PKI architecture and components means design pki so the root is protected, intermediates handle operations, and supporting services publish status and revocation cleanly.. In practical terms, how authorities, repositories, and responders form a trustworthy system. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Understanding the distinction between root and intermediate CAs is fundamental. A root CA is the ultimate trust anchor: its public key is distributed to clients as a trusted root, and any certificate chain traced back to it can be trusted. Because of this centrality, organizations typically keep root CA private keys offline and highly protected, using them only to sign intermediate CA certificates. Intermediate CAs hold certificates signed by the root and perform day-to-day issuance. This tiered approach brings operational benefits: if an intermediate is compromised, the organization can revoke that intermediate and reissue without needing to replace the root. It also allows different intermediates to enforce policy boundaries — for example, one intermediate for server certificates, another for code signing. A common misconception is that fewer CAs equals simpler security; in reality, a single online root increases risk. Tiered design balances security with operational flexibility and supports key rotation and compartmentalization. Certificate Authority roles — Root vs Intermediate means use an offline root and online intermediates to minimize compromise impact and enable operational rotation.. In practical terms, why tiered signing reduces risk and supports recovery. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The Registration Authority is an intermediary that verifies the identity of certificate requesters before the CA issues a certificate. An RA collects the Certificate Signing Request and the proof documents or authentication data needed to confirm identity, then forwards validated requests to the CA. Using an RA is a practical measure to protect the CA: the CA can remain offline or tightly restricted, while the RA performs the higher-volume identity checks. For example, an RA may validate employee directories, check ownership of a domain, or verify corporate registrations depending on the certificate type. A misconception is that the RA is optional in all deployments; while small, single-application PKIs may omit a dedicated RA, enterprise-grade PKI commonly uses RAs to centralize and auditable identity verification. An effective RA implementation includes logging, role separation, and strong process controls so that identity checks themselves cannot be bypassed or forged. Registration Authority (RA) means let the ra handle identity verification so the ca can be constrained and protected from direct operational exposure.. A Certificate Revocation List, or CRL, is a signed, timestamped list containing serial numbers of certificates that a CA has invalidated before their scheduled expiration. CAs publish CRLs at regular intervals so relying parties can download and compare certificates they encounter to the list of revoked serial numbers. Because CRLs are periodically published, there is an inherent delay between revocation and when clients download the updated list; this window creates exposure if a compromised certificate continues to be accepted until the next CRL download. CRLs are useful where clients can cache lists and where offline validation is acceptable. They are simple to implement and do not require an online responder, but they can become large in high-volume environments and increase bandwidth and processing requirements. Operational practice includes setting reasonable publication frequency, using delta CRLs where supported to reduce size, and combining CRLs with other mechanisms for timely revocation when necessary. OCSP, the Online Certificate Status Protocol, provides a way for clients to query a responder in real time about the revocation status of a specific certificate. Instead of downloading an entire list, a client asks the OCSP responder whether a certificate is good, revoked, or unknown. This reduces bandwidth and provides near real-time answers. OCSP stapling further improves performance and privacy: the server fetches a signed OCSP response from the responder and presents it during the TLS handshake. This means the client receives revocation status without contacting the OCSP responder directly, lowering latency and avoiding client-side privacy leaks. However, OCSP introduces a dependency on responder availability; if the responder is unreachable, clients and servers must have policy decisions about how to proceed. A misconception is that OCSP always eliminates staleness; while it is more timely than CRLs, its reliability depends on responder design and caching behavior. Practitioners often combine OCSP, stapling, and robust responder deployment for both timeliness and resilience. An X.509 certificate binds a public key to an identity and defines how that key may be used. Key fields include Subject — the entity the certificate represents — and Issuer — the CA that signed the certificate. The public key itself is included, plus a unique serial number the CA uses to track the certificate. Validity dates define the window during which the certificate is considered valid. The Signature Algorithm indicates how the CA signed the certificate. Extensions add policy and constraints: Subject Alternative Name allows multiple hostnames or addresses to be covered; Key Usage defines allowed cryptographic operations like digital signature or key encipherment; Extended Key Usage narrows the certificate to particular applications such as Server Authentication or Code Signing. Reading these fields helps you determine whether a certificate suits a purpose and whether a client should trust it. A common oversight is relying on expiry alone; extensions and SANs often determine whether a certificate will be accepted by clients. Three certificate extensions are especially relevant for operational compatibility: Subject Alternative Name, Key Usage, and Extended Key Usage. SAN lists all DNS names and IPs a certificate covers; if a client checks the server hostname against the certificate and the SAN does not include that name, the client will report a name mismatch. Key Usage controls cryptographic actions, for example whether a key can be used to encrypt keys or to perform a digital signature. EKU provides more explicit application-level constraints: a certificate may have EKU set to Server Authentication so it can be used for TLS, or Code Signing so it can sign binaries. Together these extensions prevent certificates from being misapplied. For instance, a code-signing certificate without Server Authentication EKU should not be trusted by a web server. A common error is relying solely on Subject CN for hostname matching; modern clients prioritize SAN and may ignore CN for multi-name certificates. When issuing certificates, ensure SAN entries and EKU align with the intended use to avoid client errors and security gaps. Choose a trust model based on scale, federation needs, and administrative control. The hierarchical model uses a single root that signs intermediates; trust flows downward and is easy to reason about — this is dominant in enterprise PKI because it centralizes authority and simplifies revocation decisions. The mesh model, or cross-certification, has CAs directly trusting each other and is useful in federated environments where peers establish bilateral trust relationships. It trades simplicity for flexibility and requires careful planning to avoid trust cycles or unexpected trust paths. The bridge model introduces a central bridge CA that connects separate hierarchies without requiring direct cross-certificates between every pair; this supports federation without collapsing local control. Each model affects certificate validation, revocation complexity, and operational procedures. For instance, cross-certification complicates revocation checks because trust paths may span multiple administrative domains. When designing an enterprise PKI, favor the hierarchical model for internal services and consider bridge patterns only when inter-organization trust is required. PKI trust models means hierarchical gives clear control and simpler revocation; mesh and bridge support federation but add complexity and planning overhead.. The certificate lifecycle has distinct stages that each require policy and operational controls. It begins with key generation and a Certificate Signing Request. The RA or CA validates identity and issues the certificate. The certificate is then distributed to the subscriber and published to a repository. During usage, the certificate participates in protocols like TLS where clients validate its chain and extensions. Before expiry, certificates should be renewed — often with a new key pair — to maintain continuity and reduce risk from long-lived keys. If compromise or role change occurs, the certificate must be revoked and that revocation published via CRL or OCSP. Finally, expiry ends the certificate’s validity. Mismanaging any stage causes outages or security incidents: failing to renew leads to service failure, while failing to revoke a compromised certificate leaves systems vulnerable. Robust lifecycle management includes monitoring impending expirations, automated renewal where appropriate, clear revocation procedures, and periodic audits. Certificate lifecycle means treat each lifecycle stage as an operational checkpoint: generate securely, verify identity, publish status, renew proactively, and revoke when needed.. Deciding between CRL and OCSP requires weighing timeliness, scalability, and availability. CRLs are simple: the CA periodically publishes a list clients download. They work well where clients can reliably fetch and cache lists and where occasionally stale status is acceptable. OCSP offers near real-time answers and is preferred when quick revocation is critical — for example, after private key compromise on a high-value server. OCSP stapling reduces client load by letting servers present a recent response during handshake, improving latency and privacy. Hybrid approaches are common: CRLs as a baseline with OCSP for critical services. Also consider delta CRLs to decrease list size. Operational constraints matter: if you cannot guarantee responder uptime or network reachability from clients, leaning on CRLs may be more dependable. Ultimately, document policies that state acceptable staleness windows, required responder redundancy, and monitoring for both methods so revocations take effect in a predictable timeframe. Remember these core ideas as you design or evaluate PKI. First, the Certificate Authority is the trust anchor; design your hierarchy so the root is protected and intermediates handle operations. Second, an RA centralizes identity vetting so the CA can remain tightly controlled. Third, X.509 certificates include critical fields and extensions — SAN, Key Usage, and Extended Key Usage — that determine which names and operations a certificate supports. Fourth, revocation must be planned: CRLs are periodic and suitable where offline lists are acceptable, while OCSP provides timely status with performance and availability implications. Finally, manage the certificate lifecycle proactively: monitor expirations, automate renewals where possible, and publish revocations immediately. These points guide secure and resilient PKI operations and prevent common failures like name mismatches, stale revocation data, and overexposed root keys.

Keep these three concise reminders: first, implement an offline root with online intermediates to reduce risk and support recovery. Second, ensure certificates include the correct SAN entries, Key Usage, and EKU so clients accept them for their intended purpose. Third, pick revocation methods that meet your timeliness and availability needs — OCSP for speed and CRLs for offline resilience — and document the policies and monitoring required. These quick references help you make pragmatic design choices during audits, deployments, and incident response. When in doubt, favor clear separation of duties and explicit policy statements that define acceptable staleness windows and responder redundancy. That discipline prevents outages and shortens the window of exposure when keys or certificates are compromised.
